newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Shares tumble, mark up as EMU delay possible.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Shares tumble, mark up as EMU delay possible.

text.p: European bourses tumbled on Friday and were depressed further by a weak start on Wall Street, but the mark benefited as investors returned to it, betting on a delay to European monetary union.

The markets have been thrown into disarray by the political storm over Bonn's intention to revalue its gold, coupled with the increasing possibility the opposition socialists will win power in France this weekend. Both developments pose serious question marks over future European economic integration.
Investors first reacted by buying the dollar, which strengthened against the mark and yen earlier in the day.

But by mid-afternoon the dollar had slipped from its peaks against the mark to just below 1.70 as the German unit recovered composure and clambered, not only against the dollar but also against the lira.
On the French elections, James McKay, international economist at Painwebber, said a clear win for the opposition Socialists, who favour a flexible EMU interpretation, would spook European markets.
"If the Socialists take an absolute majority - that would be detrimental to markets...We could see a delay or abandonment to the EMU project," he said.
Analysts said increasing possibilities for a delay to EMU, due to start in 1999, would help investment back into the mark.
"If people think there is going to be an EMU delay, they will move back into Bunds and the deutschmark will strengthen," said Sally Wilkinson, senior economist at Daiwa Europe
Against the lira, the mark hit one-month highs of 995.25, after softer Italian GDP growth and rumours of Italian rating downgradings.

On European bourses a morning slide turned into an afternoon tumble for London and Frankfurt, exacerbated by Wall Street where the Dow was more than one percent off in early New York trading, weighed down by a profits warning by from Intel Corp .

Frankfurt shares had started soft and continued to fall, with floor trading ending down almost 2.5 percent as German markets reacted after their holiday on Thursday to the row over revaluing German gold assets

On the Paris bourse, leading stocks, which have suffered badly from election jitters over the past few days, shed more than 1.5 percent within the first 10 minutes of trading, though they had recovered somewhat by mid-afternoon.
"Once again, a number of people are coming round to a probable Socialist victory," said a broker.
One victim, defence and electronics giant Thomson-CSF, was hit by prospects that the left, if it wins the election, may scrap the sale of the state's 58 percent stake.
In London, FTSE 100 blue chips, which had been falling all morning, had tumbled almost 1.4 percent by mid-afternoon as investors locked in their profits fearful of what next week may bring.
There was a view in London that a French leftwing victory at the weekend could spook bond and share markets throughout Europe on Monday.

"If the Socialists win (in France) there is bound to be a knee-jerk reaction in French and German bond and share markets on Monday which will spill over into our market," the head of trading at a major London brokerage said.
The listing on Monday of the Halifax building society, Britain's biggest mortgage lender, should prop up the financial sector helping to limit the downside, he said.
"The institutions have to have Halifax in their portfolios and the market knows it...But even that won't be enough to keep the FTSE afloat if the EMU turmoil continues."
CURRENCIES AT 1430 GMT
The dollar was quoted at 1.6989 marks and 116.10 yen compared with 1.6990 marks and 116.12 yen in late European trading on Thursday.
STOCK MARKETS AT 1400 GMT
LONDON - The FTSE-100 index was down 60.5 points at 4,612.2.
PARIS - The CAC-40 was down 14 points at 2,565.
FRANKFURT - The 30-share DAX index closed down 88.58 points at 3547.84.
PRECIOUS METALS
Gold fixed at $345.60 compared with late Thursday's London price of 344.05. Silver was at $4.80.
